utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, would the Registrar please call the case? (The Registrar called the case speaking in French)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a hearing of the motion filed on behalf of the accused General Blaskic for modification of the conditions of detention pursuant to Rule 64 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. May I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I appear for the Prosecution with my co‑counsel Mr. Gregory Kehoe. We have two assistants who will assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: I am Zvonimar Hodak. I am defence lawyer of the accused Mr. Blaskic and I am appearing here with my colleague, also a lawyer, Miss Nela Pedisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, let me just check that the technical systems are working properly. General Blaskic, can you hear me? GENERAL BLASKIC [original: Croatian]: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hodak, would you please proceed with your application?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday in a written submission I elaborated my attitude in respect of the procedural position of my client, Mr. Blaskic. I believe that since I have studied the indictment in detail all conditions have been met, all conditions provided for in Rule 64, that the President may modify the conditions of detention. So we believe that Mr. Blaskic has appeared before the Tribunal voluntarily. He has showed his goodwill to stand the trial and we apply that this be taken into consideration, and that Mr. Blaskic be enabled, in accordance with Rule 64 and Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, during the proceedings to defend himself while at liberty. In other words, Mr. Blaskic and myself believe that the facts that have been presented in the indictment speak for themselves; that he is not the perpetrator of any of the crimes which are considered as crimes against the international law. This fact should be taken into consideration and lesser conditions should be applied, and this all in accordance with Rule 64 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hodak, are you aware that we are here meeting within the framework of Rule 64 because it is this Rule which gives the President of the Tribunal the power to modify the conditions of the detention of the accused? So, therefore, you cannot rely both on 64 and 65, because 65, it is a matter which must go before the Tribunal Chamber, and it is aimed at requesting the Trial Chamber to grant provision of release. So I wonder whether you are aware that if you want to put in an application based on 65, then you have to apply to the Trial Chamber with a view to obtaining, as I say, a provision of release; whereas, in my case I can only decide upon possible modifications of the conditions of the detention of the accused. So shall we proceed on the basis that we are now meeting within the framework, as I say, of 64 only? Of course, you would have the right after the initial appearance of the accused to apply to the Trial Chamber for the possible provision of release of your client. So shall I take it that you agree that we should now confine ourselves to 64?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully agree with you. The first part of my submission that I sent to you yesterday referred to the Rules 64 and 65, but I agree that due to procedural reasons we limit ourselves today to the Rule 64 which enables you to modify the conditions of detention of my client. Of course, after that we will invoke the Rule 64 after the initial appearance of, 65 ‑‑ excuse me, 65, after the initial appearance of my client.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. May I ask you a few questions? First of all, why was the arrest warrant issued in November '95 against General Blaskic not executed in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia? Because normally when arrest warrants are issued and are sent to the relevant authorities of a particular country where the accused is residing, those authorities are duty bound to execute the arrest warrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem was the Croatian constitution and Croatian laws. Croatian administration has passed a law on the co‑operation of Croatia with the International War Crimes Tribunal. Once this law has been ratified by the Croatian Parliament there would be no problems whatsoever as far as the Republic of Croatia and its government is concerned to execute the mentioned warrants. Croatia, had it executed the warrant from 1995, Croatia would have violated the Article 10 of the Croatian constitution because a law was supposed to be passed before that, a law which would have specified who can arrest a Croatian citizen and extradite, surrender the Croatian citizen not to another country, but to an international organisation, which was eventually ‑‑ which is the International Tribunal in The Hague. There was the problem with the execution of the warrants of arrest and I think that within a month this problem will be definitely solved in Croatia, and will no longer be disputable. This was my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, if I am correct in understanding what you just said, General Blaskic was not arrested because the Croatian authorities were not entitled to execute the arrest warrant because of a lack of the appropriate legislative provisions within the Croatian legal system. As soon as this implemented legislation is passed, it will be possible to execute arrest warrants. May I now ask you what particular form of detention you are seeking under Rule 64 and for what reasons? Because, as I pointed out before, what you are now seeking is the modification of the conditions of detention of the accused. What sort of modification are you requesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: I have already tried to explain in my initial opening statement. I believe that the position of General Blaskic, as far as the procedure is concerned, is far better than the one of other indictees from the former Yugoslavia. General Blaskic was the Chief of Staff of the Croatian Defence Council in Bosnia‑Herzegovina. He was known as a General both by the Geneva Conventions relative to prisoners of war and law of war in general. We already pointed out to that in one of our submissions to Prosecutor Goldstone, and we mentioned several well known witnesses, such as journalist Roy Gutman, and other witnesses who will be able to testify that Mr. Blaskic did not act in contravention with the International War. We believe that he has proven that he is a personality with high moral principles and he is a professional soldier, unlike some other soldiers from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He completed, he graduated from a Military Academy and he knows that how to respect civilian rights and the rights of prisoners of war during the war. I was informed that the Prosecution also respect that fact. In my conversations with them, we concluded, we came to the conclusion together that it should be good to propose to you, Mr. President, to modify the conditions which are mentioned in Rule 64, because there is not a single evidence against this man that he was either a perpetrator or that he issued orders to commit war crimes. We believe that General Blaskic deserves a special treatment and we also believe that this Tribunal and you, as the President of the Tribunal, should somehow take into consideration that fact, and enable General Blaskic to defend himself while at liberty, some sort of restricted liberty. This would not be a classical type of liberty, and we know that he would not be able to move freely around The Hague and the Netherlands, but he would be under the surveillance of Dutch authorities and would be accommodated into a facility designated by Dutch authorities, and that he would be under the surveillance and the control of the Dutch security service. This is far more favourable for my client than the classical type of detention of this Tribunal. So, I, therefore, believe that those details, my Defence has already pointed out those details through the Croatian Embassy and we specified those conditions, we discussed those conditions, also with Dutch authorities. Financial means have been assured, and I believe that once again it would be right and I would ask you, as the President of the Tribunal, to accept our proposal in accordance with Rule 64.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. So, therefore, you are seeking a form of restricted liberty, as you have said, and the reasons, I understand, is because of the particular position of General Blaskic as Chief of Staff because of his personality and because you claim that there is no evidence proving that he committed the crimes with which he is charged. Your view, he deserves for this reason a special treatment. Leaving aside the matter of evidence because, of course, this, as you know, touches upon the merits of a case and this is a matter which will be dealt with by the Trial Chamber, I wonder whether you could specify, first of all, in addition to these reasons you also, as you pointed out at the outset, there is also the question that he is coming here voluntarily. Under the Croatian legislation he was not arrested. He could not be arrested, as you pointed out before, so, therefore, there is a sort of voluntary surrender by him. I think this is an added reason you pointed out at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by restricted liberty? Do you mean house arrest? You know, house of arrest, namely, that somebody should be detained, not in a prison, but in a place from which he cannot move freely, and under close police surveillance? Are you seeking house arrest or any other form of limitation or restriction on his liberty? I consulted, I went through the Croatian legislation, and I came across one particular provision of the law on criminal procedure of the Republic of Croatia. This is Article 176, where provision is made for an indictee to be asked or requested or, rather, I should say, ordered not to leave his place of residence without the permission of the court. Of course you are fully familiar, I assume, I am sure, with Article 176. So what sort of measure of detention are you requesting? House arrest or, rather, this sort of compulsory residence which, according to the Croatian legislation, I think, is not a form of detention? Could you elaborate on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am familiar with Article 176 of the Law and Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Croatia. It is a very good provision in our procedural law, whereby the accused promised that he would not go into hiding, that he would answer to all summonses issued by the court, that he would respect regulations, legal regulations, will not influence witnesses and that he will honour the agreement he has with the Tribunal in relation to Article 176. As for Mr. Blaskic, we request, we ask, that the conditions of detentions from Rule 64 be modified to the extent, to the possible extent, for the Dutch authorities. Mr. Blaskic is ready to accept all conditions imposed by the Tribunal if his request is granted, so he will accept all conditions that will be granted to him by the Tribunal. He is not going to seek asylum in the Netherlands. He will not contact the media. He will not give interviews to the press. He will not leave his place of residence and he will not leave the Netherlands without the approval of the Tribunal. Mr. Blaskic has accepted all these conditions by the very fact of his voluntary surrender to the Tribunal. As you pointed out, he did not have to appear voluntarily to the Tribunal before the passing of the relevant law by the Republic of Croatia, but he also wants to honour his own name and he is an honourable soldier. That is the reason why he came here voluntarily. This is one more fact that speaks in favour of his position. He is ready to abide by all conditions which would be set out to him by the Tribunal, and he is ready to respect all the conditions imposed by the government of the Netherlands or Dutch authorities if the Dutch authorities designate a place of residence for him here in the Netherlands. So Mr. Blaskic thinks that the very fact he came here voluntarily, he has shown goodwill to have his problem, his case solved. He believes that he has all arguments on his side; he has all evidence that he is ready to present to this Tribunal, and he has been claiming so far that he is not guilty for the crimes he is charged with in this indictment. This was the reason why he came here voluntarily, and he believes that this being the case the Tribunal can trust him if he promises that he will respect all the conditions set to him by the Tribunal and the Dutch authorities until the end of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you do not mind, Mr. Hodak, I would like to ask you a further question. So I understand General Blaskic is ready to comply with all these conditions, do these conditions also include the financial requirements which may have been set out by the Dutch authorities? Financial implications of ‑‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes, we have ensured financial means requested by the Dutch government from our sponsors, private persons, and the way we could, but whatever has been requested from us by the Dutch authorities has been ensured and there will be no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, could you please proceed with your response to this application by Mr. Hodak?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour has already dealt with Rule 65 so I will confine myself to saying something about Rule 64. As for that application, the Prosecution agrees to modifications if your Honour is satisfied that the accused has voluntarily appeared before the court today, before you today, and that all costs related the modifications and requirements of the host countries are met as now explained by Mr. Hodak. Of course, I will not go into any obvious reasons, discussion, about the evidence or anything pertaining to the case in other ways. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you are raising, Mr. Ostberg, in particular, the question of whether or not I should be satisfied that General Blaskic has appeared voluntarily before our Tribunal. I would like, therefore, to ask Mr. Hodak to give us some details about this matter because there were also in the press conflicting reports on this matter. I would like him to give me a detailed account of what happened over the last few days so as to show that actually, indeed, General Blaskic did appear here voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, we had a hearing set out for 29th March at 2.30. Unfortunately, General Blaskic could not come to that hearing, because due to some very objective reasons General Blaskic 10 days ago, actually 12 days ago, got a son and his wife was in a very difficult emotional situation in view of that, considering the fact that he had to leave and that she did not know when he would be back to Croatia. When the wife of Mr. Blaskic went over that crisis, General Blaskic called my office himself and he made himself available and he said that he wishes to appear before the Tribunal. A couple of days ago, I organised a flight, a regular flight, Zagreb/Amsterdam, and yesterday we arrived at the Zagreb airport without any escort whatsoever. General Blaskic and his wife alone, myself together with my colleague, we boarded the regular flight Zagreb/Amsterdam and we arrived in Brussels ‑‑ sorry, Amsterdam where General Blaskic was taken over by the Dutch police. The Dutch police arrested him, read out his rights, which are stipulated by the Statute of this Tribunal. This shows that General Blaskic has surrendered himself voluntarily. There are videos recordings of that you can see ‑‑ I saw them yesterday on TV ‑‑ showing General Blaskic arriving alone with his wife to the airport. There was no presence whatsoever of any police. He was not handcuffed and there was nothing which would indicate that Mr. Blaskic had to appear before this Tribunal. I do not think that this is something the Croatian government would do anyway, because the law on the co‑operation of Republic of Croatia and the Tribunal will be passed very soon, and if the Croatian government wanted to act forcibly they would have waited for this law to be passed by the Parliament, and in that case they would have all the legal means available at their disposal to hand over to surrender General Blaskic to the Tribunal. So I can assure that you General Blaskic came to this Tribunal voluntarily, and he wishes to show that the charges against him are not correct, are wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I now turn to Mr. Ostberg and ask him whether he has any means of verifying whether the Dutch authorities are satisfied with the arrangements, the financial arrangements, agreed upon and stand with Mr. Hodak?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you suggest any way of getting the views of the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because, of course, my decision would be made conditional on the Dutch authorities being satisfied with such arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I was under the impression, your Honour, that the Dutch authorities would be invited here today to just give a statement to that fact, and I think may be the Registrar or somebody else has any means to get in contact with the Dutch authorities to have this confirmed. Today or yesterday, I have not got any substantial statements saying that that is the case. I do not distrust the people saying they have any agreement, but I have not seen any.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have been informed is that the cost for the Dutch State would be 7,000 guilders a day and their requirement is that this amount would be paid monthly in advance. That is as far as I know about this financial agreement. But if it is signed between the two countries or other things, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I, first of all, specify that actually the Registry had contacted the Dutch authorities which felt that they should not appear as amicus curiae. That means I will have to satisfy myself that there is full agreement of the Dutch authorities. In any case, I may find it necessary to make my decision conditional on the consent of the Dutch authorities to this financial agreement. But may I now turn to Mr. Hodak to ask him whether he can formally state that either he or somebody else, whatever organisation and so on, is prepared to pay this monthly sum of 7,000 guilders in advance? Could you formally undertake this commitment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am familiar with the details requested by the Dutch government as condition for this. I am familiar with the sum of 7,000 guilders per month. We officially will abide by that. I can claim that 200,000 guilders have already been paid as advance for this case, in case the President of the Tribunal grants our request and modifies the conditions from Rule 64. We also have an arrangement that in case the President does not change the conditions of detentions that amount will be paid back to us, but you can check that with the Dutch authorities. That amount of money has already been paid to them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we adjourn, I would like again to come back, if you do not mind, to a point which to me is of crucial importance, namely, a distinction between what I would regard as house arrest and what I would regard as compulsory residence. So compulsory residence is to me what is provided for in Article 176 of the Croatian law on criminal procedure, namely, this is some particular treatment which applies to somebody who is not in detention. So he is free, but he is asked or requested by the relevant court to stay at home and not to move out. Why? Because the intention is to prevent his going into hiding or leaving the country. So this is something which, for instance, to my mind, could be provided for by our Tribunal, by the Trial Chamber, under Rule 65, because it is a form of provisional release under particular conditions. House arrest, by contrast, is a form of detention in a place which is not the prison but is another place where, however, somebody would be treated as a detainee. Then we can also have probably I see a third possibility of depending on the reasons justifying house arrest, whether these reasons do exist or not, a form of detention which is harsher than house arrest. However, it would be different from the detention in prison, from proper imprisonment, because the detention would take place in a place different from the prison. So, you see, I , therefore, see three different gradations, as it were: the house arrest and the confinement of a detainee under what I would regard as sort of prison conditions, however, in a place different, as I say ‑‑ I am sorry for repeating, for overemphasising, this point ‑‑ from the detention unit. This is something which I would not even regard as a house arrest. I mean, it is not a question of legal labels, but I hope that you are aware of the different kinds of detention other than the one provided for under our Rules, namely, detention or remand, detention in our prison. So may I ask you whether you are now clear in your mind about this difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Yes, I fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now turn to General Blaskic and ask him whether he would like to add any comments or any remarks? General Blaskic, may I ask you whether you would like to set out your views on this matter which, after all, regards your own status and your conditions of detention? GENERAL BLASKIC [original:Croatian]: Your Honour, I have no objections whatsoever, neither any requests additional to what my lawyer has so far stated. I just want to claim once again that I have appeared before this Tribunal voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor would like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, just a final remark: we do not deal today with anything that has anything to do with Rule 65, it is just Rule 64, and not things that your Honour can do under these provisions. Above that, I have no other comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I fully agree with you that, of course, under Rule 65 I would have no competence, no authority. It is for the Trial Chamber to pass on this matter, so I fully agree with you. But I understand that Mr. Hodak is prepared to put in a request under Rule 65. This will be put before the Trial Chamber and, of course, you are fully entitled to do so after the initial appearance of ‑‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. Any other comments, Mr. Hodak? In general, any other comments or observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be all. Once again I would request on behalf of my client that, in accordance with your powers, you modify the conditions of detention from Rule 64.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other matters, I think that the Tribunal stands adjourned until probably tomorrow. I hope to be able to hand down my decision either tonight very late because I need some time or tomorrow probably tomorrow. Thank you.
